briefOverview: An angel reveals the judgment of “Babylon the Great,” depicted as a splendid yet blood‑stained harlot riding a blasphemous beast, and explains the symbolic heads and horns that represent world powers aligned against the Lamb.
summary: One of the bowl-bearing angels shows John the coming judgment of the great harlot who sits on many waters, seducing rulers and peoples. In the wilderness John sees a richly adorned woman riding a scarlet beast with seven heads and ten horns, holding a cup of abominations; her forehead reads, “MYSTERY, BABYLON THE GREAT,” and she is drunk with the blood of the saints. The angel interprets the vision: the beast that “was, and is not, and is to ascend” heads to destruction; the seven heads are seven mountains and also seven kings, five fallen, one present, one yet to come; the beast is an eighth and belongs to the seven. The ten horns are ten future kings who for a short time give their power to the beast and together wage war against the Lamb, but the Lamb—Lord of lords and King of kings—overcomes with his called, chosen, and faithful followers. The waters signify peoples and nations. Paradoxically, those allied horns will turn on the harlot, stripping and burning her, for God has purposed their actions, and the woman is identified as the great city that rules over the earth’s kings.
externalContext: Many early Christian readers likely associated “seven mountains” with Rome, famed for its seven hills, and “Babylon” functioned as a common Jewish and Christian code-name for Rome as an oppressive imperial center. In the late first century, Roman imperial cults promoted loyalty to the emperor, creating pressure on Christians who refused participation. Legends about Nero’s return (Nero redivivus) circulated in this era, which may illuminate language about a ruler who “was and is not and is to come.” Client kings and provincial elites did, in fact, collaborate with Rome’s power, benefiting from its commerce and prestige. Revelation employs this political-religious backdrop to portray empire as spiritually seductive yet destined for divine judgment.
externalReferences: The title “Babylon” and the imagery of a golden cup making nations drunk echo prophetic oracles against historical Babylon (Jeremiah 51:7, 13; Isaiah 47:1–8). The harlotry, stripping, and burning motifs draw on covenant-infidelity judgments in Ezekiel (Ezekiel 16:35–41; 23:25–29). The beast with multiple heads and ten horns, and the ten kings, recall apocalyptic visions of empires and kings in Daniel (Daniel 7:7–8, 23–24). Within Revelation itself, the beast language and book-of-life motif connect to earlier visions (Revelation 13:1–8; 13:8) and anticipate Babylon’s fall in the next chapter (Revelation 18).

sectionTitles.title: Vision of Babylon on the Beast

practicalQuestions: Where might wealth, prestige, or political power be tempting me to compromise allegiance to the Lamb?
In what ways could my community be participating in systems that exploit or seduce the nations?
How can I cultivate discernment to see beyond spectacle and propaganda to spiritual realities?
What practices help me remain faithful when powerful forces oppose Christian witness?
How do I respond when erstwhile allies turn destructive—trusting God’s purposes without becoming cynical?
uncertainAreas: Identifying the seven kings and the timing implied by “five have fallen, one is, the other has not yet come” is debated; whether the woman/city must be Rome specifically or a transhistorical symbol of oppressive imperial power is also contested. The meaning of the beast as the “eighth” yet “of the seven,” and the nuance of the beast that “was, and is not, and is to ascend,” are difficult and may allude to contemporary myths (e.g., Nero redivivus) or symbolic cycles of empire. The duration “one hour” for the ten kings’ authority and the exact historical referents of the ten horns are likewise uncertain.
